raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to solve a persistent limitation of metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): the permanent “cage” that may impair vasomotion, complicate future bypass or re-intervention, and contribute to late inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, or thrombosis. The concept is old: the Igaki-Tamai poly-L-lactic acid stent established clinical feasibility, while the everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold became the dominant coronary BVS platform tested in modern percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [1-3]. Early ABSORB cohort studies suggested that after temporary radial support and drug delivery, scaffold resorption could permit late lumen preservation, restored vasomotion, and disappearance of struts on intravascular imaging [4-6].

The initial randomized experience was encouraging but ultimately cautionary. In ABSORB II, 1- and 2-year outcomes were broadly comparable with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents, but by 3 years the scaffold failed to show superior vasomotion or late luminal gain and had more target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [7-9]. ABSORB III met non-inferiority for 1-year target-lesion failure in selected, noncomplex lesions, yet 3-year follow-up demonstrated excess device-oriented events and thrombosis, especially in small vessels [10,11]. ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan similarly showed acceptable 1-year angiographic and clinical outcomes under trial conditions, reinforcing that early efficacy was possible when lesions were simple and sizing was controlled [12,13]. Smaller comparative studies such as EVERBIO-2 and all-comers trials such as AIDA broadened the evidence base; AIDA, in particular, demonstrated a clinically important excess of device thrombosis in routine PCI, accelerating the retreat of first-generation polymeric BVS from practice [14,15].

Several mechanisms explain this trajectory. Absorb had relatively thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, greater crossing profile, and a prolonged period during which mechanical dismantling coincided with incomplete endothelial coverage or malapposition. Implantation quality proved central: correct vessel sizing, aggressive lesion preparation, and high-pressure post-dilation—the “PSP” strategy—were associated with better outcomes in pooled ABSORB analyses [16]. Quantitative coronary angiography, intravascular ultrasound, and optical coherence tomography studies emphasized that small reference-vessel diameter, underexpansion, eccentric expansion, residual stenosis, and calcification increased adverse-event risk [17-19]. Thus, the problem was not simply “bioresorption” but the mismatch between first-generation scaffold mechanics and real-world coronary anatomy.

Meta-analyses clarified the signal. Across randomized trials, Absorb BVS increased scaffold thrombosis and target-lesion failure compared with contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents, with risk concentrated before complete resorption [20-22]. This finding reshaped clinical management: prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy was often advised after BVS, particularly when implantation was suboptimal or complex anatomy was treated, although this strategy was based more on pathophysiology and observational signals than definitive randomized evidence [23]. Reviews from the field therefore reframed BVS as a promising concept limited by first-generation execution rather than as a failed therapeutic principle [24].

Second-generation devices attempt to preserve the theoretical advantages while addressing mechanical liabilities. Magnesium-based scaffolds resorb faster and have different degradation biology. BIOSOLVE-II showed favorable early angiographic and clinical results with a sirolimus-eluting absorbable metal scaffold, and 5-year follow-up suggested sustained safety in selected lesions [25,26]. The BIOSOLVE-IV registry expanded experience in routine practice, though still largely in relatively simple lesions and large vessels [27]. Newer magnesium platforms, including DREAMS 3G, aim for thinner struts, improved deliverability, and restoration of vasomotion [28]. Long-term randomized imaging studies such as EVERBIO-2 are also important because they test whether late vascular normalization translates into outcomes beyond the early hazard window [29].

At present, BVS should not be considered a routine substitute for modern ultrathin metallic DES. Their clinical niche, if any, is likely to be young patients, focal de novo lesions in adequately sized vessels, and settings where future surgical or percutaneous access is valuable. Future trials must demonstrate not only non-inferiority during the resorption phase but also a late clinical advantage after scaffold disappearance. The key lesson from Absorb is that bioresorbability alone is insufficient: success requires thin struts, predictable degradation, radial strength without dismantling-related thrombosis, image-guided implantation, and careful lesion selection. The contemporary question is therefore not whether the “vanishing stent” is attractive, but whether newer scaffolds can vanish safely enough to justify renewed adoption [30].
